short_definition: The sunk cost fallacy is the tendency to keep investing time, money or effort into something because of what you've already spent, even when continuing no longer makes sense.
explanation: A sunk cost is money, time or effort you've already spent and can't get back, whatever you decide next. Logically, a decision should depend only on future costs and benefits. The fallacy happens when past spending drives the choice instead, as in 'I've already put two years into this, so I can't quit now.'

The sunk cost fallacy matters because it shows up everywhere: finishing a bad course because you paid for it, holding a losing investment to 'get back to even', keeping a failing side project going, or paying for repair after repair on an unreliable car. Spotting it frees up time and money for better options, which ties directly to opportunity cost.

The nuance is that persistence isn't always a mistake. Sometimes past effort really does improve your future chances, because you've built skills, an audience or momentum. The test is whether continuing is the best use of your next hour or next dollar, based only on what you expect from here on.
example: Example (illustrative numbers): You've spent $1,200 repairing an old car this year. A new repair quote is $1,500, and similar reliable used cars sell for about $4,000. The $1,200 is gone whatever you choose, so the real question is whether $1,500 on this car is better value than putting money toward a replacement, given the repairs it's likely to need. The $1,200 you've already spent shouldn't be part of the calculation.
common_mistake: Using 'I've already invested so much' as the reason to keep going, instead of asking: 'If I were starting fresh today, would I choose this?'
title: Sunk Cost Fallacy
